overview: CI/CD for data pipelines means applying the same lint -> test -> deploy discipline used for application code to dbt projects and Airflow DAGs, so that a pull request automatically validates SQL, runs data tests, parses every DAG, and only merges when the pipeline change is proven safe.

The data-specific challenge is that pipelines are stateful and depend on a warehouse and a running scheduler: a dbt CI job must build and test only the changed models in an isolated CI schema (Slim CI via state:modified+, comparing against a production manifest.json), and an Airflow CI job must import every DAG to catch parse errors before they reach the scheduler.

Deployment is not shipping a binary but promoting pipeline code across environments: dbt is deployed via dbt Cloud jobs, git-sync, or a container running dbt against a production target, while Airflow DAGs are deployed via a git-sync sidecar, a bucket sync (GCS/S3), or by baking DAGs into an image - always with dev -> stage -> prod target/profile promotion.
learningObjectives: Build a GitHub Actions dbt CI workflow that lints SQL (sqlfluff), compiles the project, and runs Slim CI (dbt build --select state:modified+) against an isolated CI schema using a production manifest.json artifact.
Build an Airflow CI workflow that imports/parses every DAG to catch broken DAGs, runs DAG-validation unit tests, and lints with ruff, then deploys DAGs on merge via git-sync or a bucket sync.

Reason about the data-specific deployment concerns: environment promotion of pipeline code (dev/stage/prod targets and profiles), isolated CI schemas, safe migrations, and the difference between deploying dbt and deploying DAGs.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: CI/CD for data pipelines is the automated build, verification, and release process applied to declarative transformation code (dbt) and workflow orchestration code (Airflow DAGs). Continuous Integration validates every pull request by linting the pipeline code, compiling/parsing it, and running data and structural tests against an isolated, non-production environment: for dbt this means compiling models, running schema and data tests, and using state comparison (state:modified+) against a production manifest to build only the changed models and their descendants in a dedicated CI schema (Slim CI); for Airflow this means importing every DAG file so parse-time errors are caught, running unit tests that assert DAG structure and integrity, and linting. Continuous Deployment promotes the validated code across environments - dbt via dbt Cloud jobs, git-sync, or containerized dbt runs targeting a production profile, and Airflow DAGs via a git-sync sidecar, object-storage sync (GCS/S3), or image baking - using per-environment targets/profiles so the same code runs against dev, staging, and production warehouses with the correct credentials and isolation.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of your data pipeline like a recipe book that a robot kitchen (the warehouse and scheduler) follows every night. CI/CD is the quality-control station that inspects every proposed change to the recipe book before it goes live. First it checks the handwriting and formatting (lint the SQL, lint the Python). Then, instead of re-cooking every dish in the whole book, it only re-cooks the dishes you actually changed - and everything that depends on them - in a separate test kitchen so it never touches the real dinner service (Slim CI in an isolated schema). For the scheduling side, it opens every recipe to make sure the robot can actually read it, because one unreadable recipe can jam the whole kitchen (DAG import test). Only when everything passes does the new recipe book get copied into the real kitchen - and even then, it goes to the practice kitchen first (staging), then the real one (production).
coreConcept.historicalContext: Airflow was created at Airbnb in 2014 by Maxime Beauchemin to express workflows as code (DAGs in Python), was open-sourced, joined the Apache Incubator in 2016, and became a top-level Apache project in 2019 - establishing 'pipelines as code, versioned in git' as the norm. dbt began around 2016 at Fishtown Analytics (later renamed dbt Labs) and popularized 'analytics engineering', bringing software practices - version control, modularity, testing, and CI - to SQL transformations in the warehouse. As teams put both DAGs and models in git, the missing piece was verifying changes cheaply: dbt Labs introduced Slim CI (deferral plus state:modified) so CI could build only changed models by comparing against a production manifest.json artifact instead of rebuilding the entire project, dramatically cutting warehouse cost and CI time. In parallel, the Airflow community standardized DAG deployment away from copying files onto schedulers toward git-sync sidecars (pull DAGs from git), object-storage sync (GCS/S3 DAGs bucket), and baking DAGs into container images. By the mid-2020s, running dbt build with state:modified in GitHub Actions against an isolated CI dataset, and parse-testing every DAG on PR, had become standard practice for data teams.

whyItMatters.business: Broken pipelines silently corrupt the numbers executives and customers rely on; automated CI that tests changed models and parses every DAG before merge means dashboards, ML features, and financial reports stay correct, protecting trust and decisions that depend on the data.
whyItMatters.engineering: Engineers get fast, safe feedback on data changes: a PR shows exactly which models changed and whether their tests pass, and a DAG that fails to import is caught in CI rather than at 2am, so reviews are trustworthy and on-call pages drop sharply.
whyItMatters.scalability: Slim CI keeps CI cost roughly constant as the project grows by building only the changed subgraph instead of thousands of models, and standardized DAG deploy (git-sync/bucket) lets hundreds of DAGs across many teams ship without hand-copying files.
whyItMatters.cost: Rebuilding an entire dbt project on every PR burns enormous warehouse credits; state:modified+ against a production manifest builds only what changed and its descendants in a small CI schema, cutting CI warehouse spend by orders of magnitude while still testing what matters.
whyItMatters.reliability: A DAG that fails to parse can jam an entire scheduler and stall unrelated pipelines; import tests plus DAG-validation unit tests, isolated CI schemas, and staged environment promotion catch these failure modes before they hit production, turning risky manual deploys into repeatable, verified releases.

coreComponents.name: dbt lint and compile stage
coreComponents.definition: The CI stage that statically checks dbt SQL style and validity - linting with sqlfluff and compiling the project (dbt parse / dbt compile) - without touching data, to catch syntax, style, and reference errors early.
coreComponents.purpose: To fail fast and cheaply on formatting and structural problems (bad Jinja, missing refs, invalid SQL) before any warehouse compute is spent on building models.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Install dbt and the adapter, run 'dbt deps' to fetch packages, lint SQL with sqlfluff (or 'dbt sqlfluff'), and run 'dbt parse'/'dbt compile' to validate the DAG of refs and macros compiles.
coreComponents.examples: sqlfluff lint models/ --dialect snowflake | dbt deps | dbt parse | dbt compile --target ci

coreComponents.name: dbt test stage (Slim CI)
coreComponents.definition: The CI stage that builds and tests only the changed models and their descendants in an isolated CI schema, using state comparison ('--select state:modified+') against a production manifest.json artifact so unchanged models are skipped.
coreComponents.purpose: To validate that changed transformations produce correct data (schema and data tests pass) at minimal warehouse cost, without rebuilding the entire project or touching production data.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Download the production manifest.json artifact, run 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts' against a per-PR CI schema, and surface failing tests as the PR status.
coreComponents.examples: dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci | dbt test --select state:modified+

coreComponents.name: Airflow DAG lint, import, and validation stage
coreComponents.definition: The CI stage that lints DAG Python (ruff), imports/parses every DAG file to catch parse-time errors, and runs unit tests asserting DAG integrity (no cycles, valid schedule, expected task ids).
coreComponents.purpose: To guarantee that every DAG the scheduler will load actually parses and is structurally valid, so a single broken DAG never jams the scheduler or blocks unrelated pipelines in production.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Run 'ruff check', import all DAGs via DagBag or a python import loop asserting zero import_errors, and run pytest DAG-validation tests (schedule set, tags present, no default retries=0, no import errors).
coreComponents.examples: ruff check dags/ | python -c 'from airflow.models import DagBag; assert not DagBag().import_errors' | pytest tests/dags/

coreComponents.name: Deploy / sync mechanism
coreComponents.definition: The mechanism that promotes validated pipeline code to each environment: for dbt via dbt Cloud jobs, git-sync, or a container running dbt against a prod target; for Airflow via a git-sync sidecar, GCS/S3 bucket sync, or baking DAGs into an image.
coreComponents.purpose: To release the tested code to dev/stage/prod deterministically using per-environment targets and profiles, so the same code runs against the correct warehouse and scheduler with the right credentials.
coreComponents.responsibilities: On merge to main, trigger the dbt production run (or update the deployed artifact) and publish DAGs to the scheduler (git-sync pull, 'gsutil rsync' / 'aws s3 sync' to the DAGs bucket, or push a new image), gated by environment promotion.
coreComponents.examples: aws s3 sync dags/ s3://airflow-dags/prod/ --delete | gsutil rsync -r dags/ gs://composer-bucket/dags/ | dbt build --target prod

internalWorking: On a pull request, dbt CI first restores the production state: it downloads the manifest.json produced by the last successful production run (stored as a CI artifact or in cloud storage), because state:modified works by diffing the current project's compiled nodes against that saved manifest to determine exactly which models changed.

The runner executes 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci': --select state:modified+ picks changed models and all their downstream descendants, --defer plus --state tells dbt to resolve refs to unchanged upstream models in the production schema rather than rebuilding them, and --target ci points at an isolated CI schema so nothing touches production.

dbt build runs models and their tests in dependency order in a single command; each model materializes into the per-PR CI schema (e.g. dbt_ci_pr_142) and its schema tests (unique, not_null, relationships) and data tests execute immediately after, so a failing test fails the whole PR with a clear node name.

Airflow CI constructs a DagBag (or imports every file under dags/) inside the same Python environment and dependency set the scheduler uses; any exception at import time - a bad import, a top-level API call, a syntax error - is recorded in DagBag.import_errors, and CI asserts that dictionary is empty, reproducing exactly what the scheduler does when it parses DAGs.

On merge to main, deployment publishes artifacts per mechanism: git-sync sidecars poll the git repo and pull the new dags/ directory into the scheduler's DAGs folder; a bucket-based setup runs 'aws s3 sync' or 'gsutil rsync' to update the DAGs bucket the scheduler watches; and dbt production runs execute 'dbt build --target prod', regenerating manifest.json which becomes the state baseline for the next round of Slim CI.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: open PR -> CI: dbt deps -> sqlfluff lint + dbt parse/compile -> download prod manifest.json artifact -> dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci (isolated CI schema) -> ruff check dags/ -> import all DAGs (assert no import_errors) -> pytest DAG-validation tests -> PR status green -> merge to main -> deploy: dbt build --target prod (regenerates manifest) + sync DAGs (git-sync / s3 sync / gcs rsync / image bake) -> scheduler picks up new DAGs -> prod pipelines run
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An engineer opens a pull request changing a dbt model (stg_orders.sql) and an Airflow DAG (orders_dag.py); GitHub Actions triggers the data CI workflow.

2. The dbt job checks out the code, runs 'dbt deps', lints with sqlfluff and runs 'dbt parse'/'dbt compile' to validate SQL and refs; it then downloads the production manifest.json artifact from the last main-branch run.

3. It runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci', which diffs against the prod manifest, builds only stg_orders and its descendants into an isolated CI schema (dbt_ci_pr_142), and runs their tests - unchanged upstream models are deferred to production, not rebuilt.

4. In parallel, the Airflow job runs 'ruff check dags/', imports every DAG asserting DagBag().import_errors is empty, and runs pytest DAG-validation tests confirming orders_dag has a schedule, tags, and no cycles; any parse failure fails the PR.

5. On merge to main, deployment runs 'dbt build --target prod' (updating the production manifest for the next Slim CI) and syncs the dags/ folder to the scheduler via git-sync or 'aws s3 sync dags/ s3://airflow-dags/prod/ --delete', after which the scheduler loads the new DAG and the pipeline runs on schedule.

keyTerminology.meaning: 'dbt build' runs models, tests, snapshots, and seeds together in dependency order, running each node's tests immediately after it is built; 'dbt test' runs only the tests (schema tests like unique/not_null and custom data tests).
keyTerminology.importance: In CI you prefer 'dbt build' over separate 'dbt run' + 'dbt test' because it interleaves building and testing in DAG order, so a failing test stops descendants and gives an accurate, fail-fast picture of the change.

keyTerminology.meaning: A dbt CI technique that selects only changed nodes and their descendants using '--select state:modified+', comparing the current project against a saved production manifest, and uses '--defer' to resolve unchanged upstream refs to production instead of rebuilding them.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the single biggest lever for cheap, fast dbt CI: instead of rebuilding thousands of models on every PR, you build only what changed and its downstream, keeping CI warehouse cost and runtime small and roughly constant.

keyTerminology.meaning: JSON files dbt writes to target/ after a run: manifest.json is the full compiled graph of every node (models, tests, sources) with checksums, and is the baseline that state comparison diffs against; run_results.json records outcomes.
keyTerminology.importance: manifest.json is what makes Slim CI possible - CI downloads the production manifest and diffs against it to compute state:modified, so managing and refreshing this artifact is central to a working dbt CI setup.

keyTerminology.meaning: A CI check that imports every DAG file (via DagBag or a python import loop) in the same environment the scheduler uses and asserts there are no import errors, catching syntax errors, missing imports, and top-level failures before deploy.
keyTerminology.importance: The scheduler parses every DAG file continuously; one file that raises at import time produces import_errors and can degrade scheduling, so a parse test is the cheapest and most important Airflow CI gate.

keyTerminology.meaning: A deployment pattern where a sidecar container (git-sync) periodically pulls the DAGs repo into the scheduler's DAGs folder; alternatives are syncing DAGs to an object-storage bucket (GCS/S3) the scheduler watches, or baking DAGs into the Airflow image.
keyTerminology.importance: It decouples 'merge to main' from 'DAGs live in the scheduler' in a controlled, auditable way, replacing fragile manual file copies and enabling per-environment DAG folders with rollback via git history.

keyTerminology.meaning: A dbt target (in profiles.yml) or an Airflow environment defines the connection, schema/dataset, and credentials for a specific environment; CI uses a 'ci' target, and promotion runs dev -> stage -> prod targets against different warehouses/datasets.
keyTerminology.importance: Per-environment targets are how the same pipeline code runs safely against isolated data - CI never touches production, staging validates against realistic data, and prod runs with production credentials and schemas.

importantConcepts.concept: Test data pipelines before deploy: dbt tests + schema tests + Airflow DAG parse tests
importantConcepts.explanation: Data CI has two distinct verification surfaces. On the dbt side you assert correctness of the data itself: schema tests declared in YAML (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) and custom data tests (singular SQL tests, dbt_utils/dbt_expectations assertions) run via 'dbt build' so a change that would produce duplicate keys or null primary keys fails the PR. On the Airflow side you assert structural correctness of the workflow code: because the scheduler parses every DAG file, the most valuable test is simply importing all DAGs and asserting no import errors, backed by unit tests that check each DAG has a schedule, sensible retries, no cycles, and expected task ids. Neither surface replaces the other - a DAG can parse perfectly while producing wrong data, and a model can be correct while its DAG fails to import - so a mature pipeline CI runs both on every PR.

importantConcepts.concept: Slim CI to test only changed models
importantConcepts.explanation: Naively, CI would run 'dbt build' on the whole project, rebuilding every model and running every test on every PR - which for a large project means thousands of models and a large warehouse bill and long runtimes. Slim CI fixes this by making CI stateful: it downloads the manifest.json from the last successful production run, then selects 'state:modified+' which resolves to only the nodes whose SQL or config changed plus all their downstream descendants (the '+' suffix). Combined with '--defer --state ./prod-artifacts', dbt resolves refs to unchanged upstream models in the production schema rather than rebuilding them, so CI materializes the minimal changed subgraph into an isolated CI schema. The trade-off is that CI depends on a fresh, correct production manifest; if the manifest is stale or missing, state comparison degrades (dbt may build more than expected or error), so refreshing and storing that artifact reliably is part of the design.

importantConcepts.concept: Deploying dbt (dbt Cloud / git-sync / artifacts) vs deploying DAGs (git-sync, S3/GCS dags, image bake)
importantConcepts.explanation: Deploying dbt and deploying Airflow DAGs are different problems. dbt is a transformation runner, so 'deploying' really means executing dbt against a production target and refreshing its artifacts: dbt Cloud jobs run 'dbt build --target prod' on a schedule or trigger, or a self-hosted setup runs dbt in a container (Airflow's KubernetesPodOperator, an ECS task, a GitHub Actions job) against prod, regenerating manifest.json that seeds the next Slim CI. Airflow DAGs, by contrast, are files the scheduler must physically load, so deploying means getting the merged dags/ directory into the scheduler's DAGs folder: a git-sync sidecar pulls the repo continuously, a bucket-based deploy runs 'aws s3 sync' / 'gsutil rsync' to the DAGs bucket the scheduler watches (Cloud Composer, MWAA), or you bake DAGs into the Airflow image for immutable, versioned deploys. Bucket/git-sync gives fast, decoupled updates; image baking gives immutability and exact reproducibility at the cost of a build-and-roll per change.

importantConcepts.concept: Environment promotion of pipeline code + safe migrations
importantConcepts.explanation: Pipeline code moves through environments the same way application code does, but the isolation is at the data layer. dbt uses targets/profiles: a 'ci' target builds ephemeral per-PR schemas, a 'stage' target runs the full project against a staging dataset with realistic data, and a 'prod' target runs against production - the same models, different connections and schemas. Airflow uses separate environments (dev/stage/prod schedulers or namespaces) each syncing DAGs from the corresponding branch or folder. The subtlety unique to data is safe migrations: because models materialize tables, a change that renames a column, changes a data type, or alters a materialization can break downstream consumers or require a full refresh. Safe promotion means testing the change against staging data first, using contracts/versioned models where consumers depend on a schema, and coordinating incremental-model 'full-refresh' runs so a structural change doesn't leave production tables in a half-migrated state.

variationsAndTypes: **dbt CI runners:** dbt Cloud CI (managed, native Slim CI with deferral to a production job) versus self-hosted CI (GitHub Actions/GitLab CI running dbt in a container, managing the manifest artifact yourself).

**dbt selection strategy:** full build (dbt build on the whole project) versus Slim CI (state:modified+ with --defer) - full for scheduled prod runs and small projects, Slim CI for PR checks on large projects.
**dbt CI isolation:** per-PR ephemeral schema (e.g. dbt_ci_pr_142, dropped after) versus a shared reusable CI schema - ephemeral gives clean isolation, shared reduces schema churn.
**Airflow DAG deploy:** git-sync sidecar (pull from git), object-storage sync (GCS/S3 DAGs bucket for Composer/MWAA), or baking DAGs into a container image - trading update speed for immutability.

**Airflow DAG validation depth:** minimal (import test only), standard (import + ruff + structure assertions), or deep (import + unit tests mocking operators + integration tests with a test scheduler).
**dbt deploy trigger:** scheduled dbt job (nightly build), CI-triggered on merge, or orchestrated by Airflow (KubernetesPodOperator running dbt) so the DAG owns the dbt run.
**Environment topology:** two-tier (CI + prod) for small teams versus three-tier (dev -> stage -> prod targets/profiles) with staging validation on realistic data for larger organizations.
advantages: **Cheap, fast feedback:** Slim CI builds only changed models in an isolated schema, so PR checks run in minutes and cost a fraction of a full build while still testing what matters.
**Catches broken pipelines pre-deploy:** DAG import tests stop parse errors before they reach the scheduler, and dbt tests catch data-correctness regressions before they corrupt production tables.
**Safe, repeatable deploys:** environment promotion with per-environment targets/profiles and git-sync/bucket deploys turns risky manual file copies into auditable, rollback-able releases.
**Trustworthy reviews:** every PR shows exactly which models changed and whether their tests pass, so reviewers and stakeholders can trust that a merge won't silently break the numbers.
disadvantages: **Manifest/state management overhead:** Slim CI depends on a fresh, correctly stored production manifest.json; a stale or missing artifact makes state comparison misbehave and requires operational care.
**CI warehouse credentials and isolation setup:** CI needs warehouse access and an isolated schema/dataset with cleanup, adding security and housekeeping complexity beyond typical app CI.
**Data tests can be flaky or slow:** tests that scan large tables or depend on data volume can be slow or intermittently fail, requiring sampling, thresholds, or scoping to changed models.

**Deploy coupling and migration risk:** structural model changes (renames, type changes, materialization switches) can break downstream consumers and need coordinated migrations that CI alone cannot fully guarantee.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use full data CI/CD (lint, Slim CI dbt tests, DAG import/validation tests, environment-promoted deploys) for any shared, production-facing analytics project where correctness of the data and reliability of the scheduler matter and multiple people change pipelines; Slim CI specifically pays off as the dbt project grows past a few dozen models.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: For a tiny prototype project with a handful of models and one DAG, full Slim CI machinery (manifest artifacts, deferral, per-PR schemas) is overkill - a simple full 'dbt build' and a DAG import test are enough; avoid heavy per-PR ephemeral schemas when a small shared CI schema serves fine, and avoid image-baked DAG deploys when fast git-sync updates are all you need.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of a publishing house releasing a new edition of an encyclopedia that thousands of people rely on. CI/CD is the editorial and printing pipeline. When an author changes one article, the copy editor doesn't re-proof the entire encyclopedia - they proof the changed article and every cross-reference that points to it (Slim CI, state:modified+), and they do this on galley proofs in a back room, never on the shelved copies (an isolated CI schema, not production). Separately, a technical checker opens every article to make sure it will actually render on the press - a single malformed article could jam the whole print run (the DAG import test). Fact-checkers verify claims against sources (dbt data tests). Only after all checks pass does the edition go first to a small review print (staging), then to the full run (production) - and every past edition is archived so a bad release can be pulled and the previous one reinstated (git history and rollback).

commonMisconceptions.myth: dbt CI should rebuild the whole project on every pull request so nothing is missed.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Rebuilding everything is slow and expensive and rarely necessary. Slim CI ('state:modified+' with '--defer' against a production manifest) builds only the changed models and their downstream descendants in an isolated schema, which is exactly the set a change can affect - unchanged models are unaffected and are deferred to production, not rebuilt.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If an Airflow DAG's tasks run fine, the DAG is safe to deploy - a parse test is redundant.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The scheduler must parse every DAG file continuously, and a file that raises at import time (bad import, top-level API call, syntax error) produces import_errors that can degrade scheduling for unrelated DAGs. Running tasks proves runtime behavior; the import/parse test proves the scheduler can even load the file, which is a different and essential guarantee.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Keep CI cost near-constant as the dbt project grows by always using state:modified+ with deferral so only the changed subgraph builds; shard Airflow DAG tests and use a DagBag import across all files in one process to parse hundreds of DAGs quickly.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Store the production manifest.json as a durable artifact (cloud storage or a pinned CI artifact) and refresh it on every production run so state comparison is always accurate; make DAG import tests non-negotiable gates so no unparseable DAG ever merges.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Isolate CI in per-PR schemas/datasets that are dropped after the run so a failed CI build leaves no residue in production; make dbt runs idempotent and use '--full-refresh' deliberately so a retried deploy converges rather than corrupts.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Publish dbt run_results.json and test outcomes as PR status and to a data-observability tool; alert on production dbt job failures and on scheduler import_errors, and track CI duration and warehouse cost to catch regressions.
productionConsiderations.security: Give CI a least-privilege warehouse role scoped to the CI schema/dataset only, store warehouse and git credentials in the CI secret store (never in profiles.yml), and use OIDC/short-lived cloud credentials for the deploy step that writes to the DAGs bucket.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Slim CI is the primary cost lever; additionally cache 'dbt deps' and Python installs, use a small CI warehouse, drop per-PR schemas promptly, and avoid full-refresh in CI so incremental models test cheaply.
productionConsiderations.performance: Parallelize dbt with '--threads', run dbt and Airflow CI jobs concurrently, cache dependencies, and keep DAG top-level code light (no heavy imports or API calls) so both the CI parse and the scheduler parse stay fast.

codeExamples.title: GitHub Actions: dbt Slim CI on pull requests (lint, compile, build changed models)
codeExamples.overview: A GitHub Actions workflow triggered on PRs that installs dbt, runs deps, lints with sqlfluff, compiles the project, downloads the production manifest.json, and runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer' against an isolated CI schema so only changed models and their descendants are built and tested.
codeExamples.code:
name: dbt-ci
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  dbt-slim-ci:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      DBT_PROFILES_DIR: ./
      # per-PR isolated schema so CI never touches production
      DBT_CI_SCHEMA: dbt_ci_pr_${{ github.event.number }}
      SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT }}
      SNOWFLAKE_USER: ${{ secrets.CI_SNOWFLAKE_USER }}
      SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.CI_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"

      - name: Install dbt
        run: pip install dbt-snowflake==1.8.* sqlfluff==3.*

      - name: dbt deps
        run: dbt deps

      - name: Lint SQL with sqlfluff
        run: sqlfluff lint models/ --dialect snowflake

      - name: Compile project (parse refs and Jinja)
        run: dbt compile --target ci

      # Restore the manifest from the last successful production run
      - name: Download production manifest artifact
        run: |
          mkdir -p prod-artifacts
          aws s3 cp s3://dbt-artifacts/prod/manifest.json prod-artifacts/manifest.json

      # Slim CI: build ONLY changed models + descendants, defer unchanged upstream to prod
      - name: dbt build (state:modified+)
        run: |
          dbt build \
            --select state:modified+ \
            --defer --state ./prod-artifacts \
            --target ci
codeExamples.breakdown: The workflow triggers on PRs to main. It installs a pinned dbt adapter and sqlfluff, runs 'dbt deps' to fetch packages, then lints and compiles (catching style and ref errors with no warehouse cost). It downloads the production manifest.json from S3 - the baseline for state comparison - then runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci': state:modified+ selects changed nodes plus their descendants, --defer resolves unchanged upstream refs to production instead of rebuilding, and --target ci points at the isolated per-PR schema. CI credentials are a least-privilege role, injected from secrets.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:

codeExamples.commonIssues: A stale or missing production manifest makes state:modified select the wrong set (or everything) - refresh it on every prod run. Forgetting --defer causes dbt to try to build unchanged upstream models and fail on missing refs. The CI role lacking CREATE SCHEMA on the CI database. Not scoping sqlfluff to changed files, making lint slow on large projects.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Cache pip and 'dbt deps' between runs; raise --threads for parallelism; drop the per-PR schema in a cleanup step or with a scheduled reaper; store the manifest as a versioned artifact so you can pin CI to a specific prod state; run sqlfluff only on files changed in the PR (git diff) for speed.

codeExamples.title: GitHub Actions: Airflow DAG lint + import test on PR, deploy DAGs on merge
codeExamples.overview: A workflow with two jobs: on PRs it lints DAGs with ruff, imports every DAG asserting there are no import errors, and runs pytest DAG-validation tests; on push to main it deploys the dags/ folder to the scheduler by syncing to the S3/GCS DAGs bucket.
codeExamples.code:
name: airflow-ci-cd
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  validate-dags:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - name: Install Airflow + deps
        run: pip install "apache-airflow==2.9.*" ruff pytest -r requirements.txt

      - name: Lint DAGs with ruff
        run: ruff check dags/

      # Parse EVERY DAG the scheduler will load; fail if any import error
      - name: DAG import test
        run: |
          python -c "
          from airflow.models import DagBag
          db = DagBag(dag_folder='dags/', include_examples=False)
          assert not db.import_errors, f'DAG import errors: {db.import_errors}'
          print(f'Parsed {len(db.dags)} DAGs with no import errors')
          "

      - name: DAG validation unit tests
        run: pytest tests/dags/ -q

  deploy-dags:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write   # OIDC for short-lived cloud creds
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Configure AWS credentials (OIDC)
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AIRFLOW_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: us-east-1

      # Deploy: sync DAGs to the bucket the scheduler (MWAA/Composer) watches
      - name: Sync DAGs to prod bucket
        run: aws s3 sync dags/ s3://airflow-dags/prod/ --delete
codeExamples.breakdown: The validate-dags job runs only on PRs: it installs Airflow with the project's requirements (so imports match the scheduler), lints with ruff, then builds a DagBag over dags/ and asserts import_errors is empty - reproducing what the scheduler does when it parses DAGs - and runs pytest structure tests. The deploy-dags job runs only on push to main: it assumes a deploy role via OIDC (short-lived credentials) and runs 'aws s3 sync dags/ s3://airflow-dags/prod/ --delete', updating the DAGs bucket MWAA/Composer watches. For GCS the deploy step would be 'gsutil rsync -r dags/ gs://composer-bucket/dags/'.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Parsed 37 DAGs with no import errors
============================= test session starts =============================
tests/dags/test_dag_integrity.py ....                                    [100%]
============================== 4 passed in 3.1s ===============================
# on merge:
upload: dags/orders_dag.py to s3://airflow-dags/prod/orders_dag.py
upload: dags/customers_dag.py to s3://airflow-dags/prod/customers_dag.py
codeExamples.commonIssues: Installing a different Airflow/provider version than the scheduler, so imports pass in CI but fail in prod - pin to match. Heavy top-level code (API calls, DB connections) in DAGs slows parsing and can fail import tests. Forgetting '--delete' on s3 sync so removed DAGs linger in the bucket. Long-lived AWS keys in secrets instead of OIDC.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Pin Airflow and provider versions to exactly match the deployed environment; add DAG-validation tests (schedule set, retries > 0, tags present, no cycles) as pytest fixtures over the DagBag; cache pip; for immutable deploys bake DAGs into the image instead of syncing; deploy to a staging environment first, then promote to prod.

codeExamples.title: Local commands: run and verify dbt and Airflow checks before pushing
codeExamples.overview: The exact commands an engineer runs locally to reproduce CI: install dbt packages, lint SQL, build and test the changed models, then lint DAGs and run the DAG import test - catching failures before opening a PR.
codeExamples.code:
# --- dbt: reproduce CI locally against a personal dev schema ---
$ dbt deps
Installing dbt-labs/dbt_utils
  Installed from version 1.1.1

$ sqlfluff lint models/staging/stg_orders.sql --dialect snowflake
All Finished!

# Build only what you changed + descendants, using your latest prod manifest
$ dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target dev
15:04:11  Found 214 models, 512 tests, 18 sources, 0 exposures
15:04:12  Concurrency: 4 threads (target='dev')
15:04:13  1 of 4 OK created sql view model dev_you.stg_orders ..... [OK in 1.1s]
15:04:14  2 of 4 PASS not_null_stg_orders_order_id ............... [PASS in 0.7s]
15:04:15  Done. PASS=4 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=4

# Run just the tests for changed models
$ dbt test --select state:modified+ --state ./prod-artifacts --target dev
15:05:02  Done. PASS=3 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=3

# --- Airflow: lint + parse DAGs the way the scheduler will ---
$ ruff check dags/
All checks passed!

$ airflow dags list
dag_id          | fileloc                    | owners | is_paused
================+============================+========+==========
customers_dag   | /dags/customers_dag.py     | data   | False
orders_dag      | /dags/orders_dag.py        | data   | False

# DAG import test: fail loudly if any DAG cannot be parsed
$ python -c "from airflow.models import DagBag; db=DagBag('dags/', include_examples=False); assert not db.import_errors, db.import_errors; print(f'OK: {len(db.dags)} DAGs parsed')"
OK: 37 DAGs parsed
codeExamples.breakdown: 'dbt deps' fetches packages. 'sqlfluff lint' checks SQL style. 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target dev' reproduces Slim CI locally against your personal dev schema, building only changed models and deferring unchanged upstream to prod. 'dbt test --select state:modified+' runs just the tests for changed models. On the Airflow side, 'ruff check' lints, 'airflow dags list' confirms the DAGs are discoverable, and the one-line python DagBag import asserts there are no parse errors - exactly the check CI runs.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Done. PASS=4 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=4
All checks passed!
OK: 37 DAGs parsed
codeExamples.commonIssues: Running without a local copy of the prod manifest, so state:modified has nothing to diff against (fetch it first). Pointing --target at a shared schema and colliding with a teammate. Missing provider packages so 'airflow dags list' or the import test fails locally but the DAG is actually fine. Forgetting to activate the project virtual environment before running.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep a small 'make ci-local' target that runs these commands so local and CI match; store a fresh prod manifest in ./prod-artifacts and refresh it periodically; scope sqlfluff and dbt selection to changed files for speed; add the DagBag import check as a pre-commit hook so broken DAGs never even get committed.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An analytics team ships dbt model changes and Airflow DAG changes to production several times a day. Twice this quarter a broken DAG that failed to parse jammed the scheduler at night and stalled unrelated pipelines, and once a model change with a missing not_null test shipped duplicate order rows into the finance dashboard. They also burn thousands of warehouse credits because every PR rebuilds the entire dbt project. They want automated CI that tests only changed models cheaply, guarantees every DAG parses before deploy, and promotes changes safely to production.
endToEndExample.inputData: A git monorepo with a dbt/ project (214 models, 512 tests, sources over Snowflake) and an dags/ directory (37 Airflow DAGs on MWAA). A production manifest.json is published to s3://dbt-artifacts/prod/ after each production dbt run. GitHub Actions runs CI; secrets hold a least-privilege CI Snowflake role and an OIDC deploy role.
endToEndExample.architecture: PR -> GitHub Actions: [dbt job] deps -> sqlfluff lint -> dbt compile -> download prod manifest -> dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --target ci (schema dbt_ci_pr_N); [airflow job] ruff -> DagBag import test -> pytest DAG validation. Merge to main -> [deploy] dbt build --target prod (regenerates + publishes manifest) + aws s3 sync dags/ to the MWAA DAGs bucket. Targets: ci -> stage -> prod profiles isolate data per environment.
processingSteps: 1. An engineer opens a PR changing stg_orders.sql (adding a not_null test) and orders_dag.py; GitHub Actions triggers the dbt and Airflow CI jobs in parallel.

2. The dbt job runs deps, sqlfluff lint, and 'dbt compile', then downloads s3://dbt-artifacts/prod/manifest.json and runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci', building stg_orders and its descendants into schema dbt_ci_pr_142 and running their tests.
3. The Airflow job runs 'ruff check dags/', builds a DagBag asserting no import_errors, and runs pytest DAG-validation tests confirming orders_dag has a schedule, retries, and no cycles.
4. Both jobs pass; the PR shows green with the list of changed models and test results, a reviewer approves, and the PR is merged to main.

5. On merge, the deploy job runs 'dbt build --target prod' (regenerating and publishing manifest.json for the next Slim CI) and 'aws s3 sync dags/ s3://airflow-dags/prod/ --delete'; MWAA loads the updated DAG and the pipeline runs on its next schedule.
endToEndExample.output: A merged, deployed change: stg_orders rebuilt in production with its new not_null test enforced, the updated orders_dag live in the scheduler, and a refreshed production manifest that becomes the state baseline for subsequent PRs.
endToEndExample.monitoring: CI posts dbt test results and run_results.json to the PR and a data-observability tool; production dbt job failures and MWAA import_errors alert PagerDuty; a dashboard tracks CI duration, warehouse credits per PR, and DAG parse time to catch regressions.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If dbt tests fail, the PR is blocked with the failing node name; if any DAG fails to import, the Airflow job fails before deploy. On deploy failure, the previous DAGs remain in the bucket (rollback by reverting the merge and re-syncing) and dbt runs are idempotent so a retried prod build converges; the per-PR CI schema is dropped by a cleanup step regardless of outcome.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Broken DAGs never reach the scheduler, data-correctness regressions are caught by tests on the changed models before merge, and CI warehouse cost drops sharply because only the changed subgraph is built - turning risky, expensive manual deploys into fast, cheap, verified releases.

industryUseCases.company: A fintech analytics engineering team on Snowflake + dbt Cloud
industryUseCases.problem: Full dbt project builds on every PR cost thousands of Snowflake credits and took 40+ minutes, and analysts occasionally merged models that broke downstream finance tables.
industryUseCases.solution: They adopted dbt Cloud CI with native Slim CI - PRs defer to a production job's manifest and run 'dbt build' on state:modified+ into a per-PR schema - plus enforced schema and data tests as required checks before merge.
industryUseCases.benefits: CI runtime and warehouse cost dropped by roughly an order of magnitude, and no untested model change reached production because failing tests block the PR.

industryUseCases.company: A media company running Airflow on Cloud Composer (GCS DAGs)
industryUseCases.problem: Engineers copied DAGs to the Composer bucket manually, and a badly-formed DAG once produced import_errors that degraded scheduling for dozens of unrelated pipelines overnight.
industryUseCases.solution: They moved to GitHub Actions that import every DAG via DagBag on each PR (failing on any import error) and, on merge, run 'gsutil rsync -r dags/ gs://composer-bucket/dags/' to deploy - with a staging Composer environment promoted before prod.
industryUseCases.benefits: Unparseable DAGs are caught in CI instead of at night, deploys are auditable through git history, and scheduler stability incidents effectively stopped.

industryUseCases.company: A retail data platform team self-hosting Airflow on Kubernetes with dbt
industryUseCases.problem: They needed both DAG and dbt changes validated together and deployed consistently across dev/stage/prod without a managed dbt Cloud plan.
industryUseCases.solution: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runs ruff + DagBag import tests and dbt Slim CI (managing manifest.json in S3) on PRs; deploys use a git-sync sidecar for DAGs and a KubernetesPodOperator that runs dbt against per-environment targets promoted dev -> stage -> prod.
industryUseCases.benefits: One CI/CD pipeline covers both tools, environment promotion isolates data safely, and git-sync gives fast, rollback-able DAG deploys without vendor lock-in.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Slim CI keeps dbt CI cost and runtime roughly constant as the project grows because only the changed subgraph builds; DAG validation scales by parsing all files in a single DagBag process and sharding heavier unit tests. Production dbt runs scale with warehouse size and --threads, and DAG deploy scales via bucket/git-sync that many DAGs and teams share.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Per-PR isolated CI schemas mean a failed CI build leaves no production residue and is dropped by cleanup. dbt runs are idempotent so retries converge, and '--full-refresh' is used deliberately for structural changes. DAG deploys are recoverable: the previous bucket contents or git commit is the rollback, and git-sync re-pulls a reverted state.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Deploy mechanisms decouple release from availability: git-sync and bucket sync update DAGs without restarting the scheduler, and dbt production runs are orchestrated jobs that can be retried. Managed platforms (dbt Cloud, MWAA, Composer) provide HA schedulers; self-hosted Airflow runs multiple schedulers.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Everything is in git - models, DAGs, profiles, CI config - so the pipeline is rebuildable from source. The production manifest.json is stored durably in cloud storage as the state baseline, DAG buckets are versioned, and warehouse tables can be regenerated by re-running dbt with --full-refresh from the recovered code.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Cache pip and 'dbt deps'; run dbt and Airflow CI jobs concurrently; raise dbt --threads; scope sqlfluff and dbt selection to changed files; keep DAG top-level code light so both CI parse and scheduler parse are fast; use a right-sized CI warehouse rather than the production one.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Slim CI is the dominant lever - build only state:modified+ and defer the rest. Additionally: drop per-PR schemas promptly, avoid --full-refresh in CI, use a small CI warehouse that auto-suspends, cache dependencies, and prefer bucket/git-sync deploys over expensive image rebuilds when immutability isn't required.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: CI uses a least-privilege warehouse role scoped to the CI schema/dataset only; warehouse and git credentials live in the CI secret store, never in committed profiles.yml; the deploy step uses OIDC/short-lived cloud credentials to write to the DAGs bucket; secrets are injected via env vars and env_var() in profiles, and PRs from forks do not receive production secrets.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Publish dbt run_results.json and test outcomes to the PR and a data-observability platform (freshness, test pass rates), alert on production dbt job failures and scheduler import_errors, and track CI metrics (duration, warehouse credits per PR, DAG parse time) to detect drift and cost regressions.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: dbt schema tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) and custom/singular data tests run via 'dbt build' on changed models in CI; packages like dbt_expectations add distributional checks. Model contracts and versions guard schema changes for downstream consumers, and freshness tests on sources validate inputs.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: CI logs each stage (lint, compile, build, test, import test, deploy) so failures are diagnosable from the PR; production dbt and Airflow emit structured logs to the platform's log store, with alerts routed to Slack/PagerDuty on test failures, DAG import errors, task failures, and deploy-step failures.

recommendedPractices: **Always use Slim CI:** build only 'state:modified+' with '--defer --state' against a fresh production manifest, into an isolated CI schema - never rebuild the whole project on PRs.
**Make the DAG import test a required gate:** parse every DAG (DagBag) and fail the PR on any import_errors so no unparseable DAG can reach the scheduler.
**Isolate CI from production:** use a per-PR (or dedicated) CI schema/dataset and a least-privilege CI warehouse role, and drop CI schemas after the run.
**Promote across environments:** use per-environment dbt targets/profiles and separate Airflow environments, validating on staging before production for risky/structural changes.
engineeringStandards: Pin dbt, adapter, Airflow, and provider versions in CI to exactly match the deployed environment so imports and builds behave identically.
Refresh and durably store manifest.json on every production dbt run so state comparison is always accurate.
Run 'dbt build' (not separate run + test) in CI so tests execute in DAG order and fail fast on the changed subgraph.
designRecommendations: Keep DAG top-level code lightweight (no heavy imports, DB connections, or API calls at parse time) so both CI and the scheduler parse fast and reliably.
Choose the DAG deploy mechanism deliberately: git-sync/bucket for fast decoupled updates, image baking for immutable versioned deploys.
Add dbt tests (at minimum unique + not_null on primary keys) and DAG-validation tests (schedule, retries, no cycles, tags) as part of the definition of done.
namingConventions: Name CI schemas predictably and per-PR (e.g. dbt_ci_pr_142) so they are easy to isolate, find, and reap.
Name dbt targets by environment (dev, ci, stage, prod) in profiles.yml so the running environment is unambiguous.
Give DAGs consistent dag_ids and tags (team/domain) so ownership and filtering are clear in the UI and tests.
documentationStandards: Document how the production manifest is produced and where it lives, since Slim CI depends on it.
Document the environment promotion path (dev -> stage -> prod targets/profiles) and how deploys are triggered and rolled back.
Document required CI secrets and the least-privilege roles used for CI and deploy.
testingStrategies: dbt: schema tests + singular data tests run via 'dbt build --select state:modified+' in CI, with contracts/versions for consumer-facing models.
Airflow: import/parse test over all DAGs (assert no import_errors) plus pytest structure tests (schedule, retries, cycles, task ids) mocking operators.
Reproduce CI locally with a 'make ci-local' target and a pre-commit DagBag import hook so failures are caught before pushing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deploying Airflow DAGs that fail to parse, jamming the scheduler.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers test that tasks run but never verify the DAG file imports cleanly, and CI lacks an import/parse gate, so a bad import or top-level error slips through.
commonMistakes.impact: The scheduler records import_errors and can degrade or stall scheduling for unrelated DAGs, causing overnight incidents and missed SLAs.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Make a DagBag import test (assert not DagBag().import_errors) a required CI check on every PR, run it locally/pre-commit, and pin Airflow/provider versions to match the scheduler.

commonMistakes.mistake: Building all dbt models on every PR instead of using Slim CI.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is the simplest thing to configure ('dbt build') and feels safest, and teams don't set up the manifest artifact and deferral needed for state comparison.
commonMistakes.impact: CI is slow (tens of minutes) and burns large amounts of warehouse credits per PR, discouraging frequent small changes and inflating cost.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Adopt Slim CI: publish a production manifest.json, and run 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts' so only changed models and descendants build.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running CI against the production schema instead of an isolated CI schema.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Reusing the prod target is quick and avoids setting up a separate schema and role, and engineers underestimate the blast radius.
commonMistakes.impact: CI builds can overwrite or corrupt production tables, tests may read half-built data, and a failed PR can leave production in a broken state.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use a dedicated per-PR (or dedicated) CI schema/dataset and a least-privilege CI role, with --target ci in profiles.yml, and drop the schema after the run.

commonMistakes.mistake: Merging models with no dbt tests, so broken data ships silently.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Writing tests feels optional and slows the PR, and without required test gates a model with no assertions passes CI trivially.
commonMistakes.impact: Data-correctness regressions (duplicate keys, null primary keys, broken relationships) reach production dashboards and ML features undetected, eroding trust.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Require at least unique + not_null on primary keys and relationship tests on foreign keys, run them via 'dbt build' in CI, and treat failing tests as a merge blocker.

comparisonSection.explanation: Full build rebuilds and tests every model on every PR - simple to configure and guaranteed complete, but slow and expensive as the project grows, since a one-line change re-runs thousands of models. Slim CI compares the project against a saved production manifest and builds only 'state:modified+' (changed nodes plus descendants) with '--defer' resolving unchanged upstream refs to production, so CI touches only what a change can affect at a fraction of the cost and time. Slim CI needs a fresh manifest artifact and correct deferral setup; use full build only for small projects or scheduled production runs, and Slim CI for PR checks on any non-trivial project.

git-sync (a sidecar pulling the DAGs repo) and bucket sync ('aws s3 sync' / 'gsutil rsync' to the DAGs bucket) update DAGs quickly and decoupled from the scheduler, with rollback via git history or bucket versioning - ideal for frequent DAG changes and managed platforms (MWAA/Composer). Baking DAGs into the Airflow container image gives immutable, exactly-reproducible deploys where code and DAGs ship together and rollback is redeploying a previous image, but every DAG change requires an image build and roll, which is slower. Choose git-sync/bucket for fast iteration and image baking when immutability, version pinning, and reproducibility outweigh deploy speed.

dbt Cloud CI is managed: it provides native Slim CI (deferral to a production job's manifest, per-PR schemas) with minimal setup, a UI, and integrated scheduling, at the cost of a subscription and some vendor coupling. Self-hosted CI (GitHub Actions/GitLab CI) runs dbt in a container where you manage the manifest artifact, isolated schema, and credentials yourself - more setup and moving parts, but full control, no per-seat cost, and easy integration with the rest of your CI (including Airflow DAG checks in the same pipeline). Choose dbt Cloud for speed-to-value and managed Slim CI; choose self-hosted for control, cost, or to unify dbt and Airflow CI in one system.

beginnerQuestions.question: Why do we run an import/parse test on Airflow DAGs in CI?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Because the scheduler must parse every DAG file continuously, and a file that raises at import time (bad import, syntax error, top-level failure) produces import_errors that can degrade scheduling for unrelated DAGs. The import test builds a DagBag over all DAGs and asserts there are no import errors, catching broken DAGs before they ever reach the scheduler.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize that the test reproduces exactly what the scheduler does at parse time, and that it is a different guarantee from tasks running correctly. Mention it should be a required PR gate.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does 'dbt build' do, and why prefer it over 'dbt run' plus 'dbt test' in CI?
beginnerQuestions.answer: 'dbt build' runs models, tests, snapshots, and seeds together in dependency order, running each node's tests immediately after it is built. In CI you prefer it because it interleaves building and testing in DAG order, so a failing test stops descendants and you get an accurate, fail-fast result for the change rather than building everything and testing separately.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Show you understand build = run + test + snapshot + seed in DAG order. Mention it pairs naturally with state:modified+ selection in CI.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does Slim CI work and what does it depend on?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Slim CI selects only changed models and their descendants using '--select state:modified+', comparing the current project against a saved production manifest.json, and uses '--defer --state' so unchanged upstream refs resolve to production instead of being rebuilt. CI then builds just that subgraph into an isolated CI schema. It depends on having a fresh, correct production manifest stored durably, because state comparison diffs against it.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Cover state:modified+, deferral, the manifest artifact, and the isolated schema. Note the failure mode when the manifest is stale or missing.

intermediateQuestions.question: What are the main ways to deploy Airflow DAGs, and how do they differ?
intermediateQuestions.answer: git-sync uses a sidecar that pulls the DAGs repo into the scheduler's folder; bucket sync runs 'aws s3 sync' or 'gsutil rsync' to a DAGs bucket the scheduler watches (MWAA/Composer); and image baking bundles DAGs into the Airflow container image. git-sync and bucket sync give fast, decoupled updates with git/bucket-versioned rollback; image baking gives immutable, exactly-reproducible deploys at the cost of a build-and-roll per change.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Contrast update speed vs immutability, and mention rollback stories for each. Tie bucket sync to managed platforms.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you keep dbt CI cheap and correct on a large project while avoiding false negatives?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use Slim CI (state:modified+ with --defer) against a fresh production manifest so only the changed subgraph builds, in a per-PR isolated schema with a least-privilege role. Keep correctness by refreshing the manifest on every prod run (so state comparison is accurate), running 'dbt build' so tests run in DAG order, and including descendants with '+'. Avoid false negatives by not deferring away tests that should run on changed models and by pinning versions so CI matches prod.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show the cost lever (Slim CI) balanced against correctness (fresh manifest, descendants, build order, version pinning) and isolation.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you handle a dbt model change that renames a column or changes a materialization safely through CI/CD?
advancedQuestions.answer: Treat it as a migration: test the change against staging data first, use model contracts/versions so downstream consumers depend on a stable schema, and coordinate a deliberate '--full-refresh' for incremental models so the table isn't left half-migrated. In CI, the change builds into an isolated schema so nothing production is affected; promotion runs stage before prod, and downstream models/tests catch breakages before merge.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Emphasize contracts/versions, staging validation, deliberate full-refresh, and environment promotion for structural changes.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your dbt CI has started rebuilding the entire project on every PR again - runtime jumped from 4 minutes to 45 and warehouse credits spiked. Slim CI was working last week. What do you investigate and fix?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Slim CI selects state:modified+ by diffing against the production manifest. If it's suddenly building everything, state comparison is failing - most likely the manifest is stale, missing, or being downloaded incorrectly, or --defer/--state was dropped, or a global change (a macro, dbt_project.yml, or package) marks all nodes modified. I'd check the CI logs for how many nodes are selected and whether the manifest download step succeeded.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Confirm the production manifest.json is being downloaded and is fresh; a missing/empty manifest makes state:modified select everything. Verify the build command still includes '--select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts'. Check whether a recent change touched a global file (macro, dbt_project.yml config, or a package version) which legitimately marks many nodes modified. Fix by restoring/refreshing the manifest publish on prod runs, re-adding deferral, and if a global change caused it, accept the larger build for that PR or scope the config change. Add an assertion/alert on the selected-node count to catch regressions early.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a CI/CD pipeline for a data platform with a large dbt project on Snowflake and 100+ Airflow DAGs on Kubernetes, used by several teams shipping changes daily.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: One CI pipeline (GitHub Actions) with parallel jobs. dbt job: deps, sqlfluff lint, dbt compile, download prod manifest from S3, 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state --target ci' into a per-PR schema with a least-privilege CI role. Airflow job: ruff, DagBag import test (assert no import_errors), pytest DAG-validation tests. On merge to main: run 'dbt build --target prod' (regenerate + publish manifest) and deploy DAGs via git-sync sidecar; promote dev -> stage -> prod via per-environment targets/profiles and namespaces. Store manifest durably; drop per-PR schemas via a reaper.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Slim CI cuts cost/time but adds manifest-management complexity and depends on a fresh artifact. Self-hosted CI (vs dbt Cloud) unifies dbt+Airflow checks and avoids per-seat cost but you own more moving parts. git-sync gives fast deploys with git rollback; image baking would give immutability at higher deploy cost. Per-PR schemas isolate cleanly but need reaping; a shared CI schema is simpler but less isolated.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Keep dbt CI cost near-constant with Slim CI as models grow; parse all DAGs in one DagBag process and shard heavier tests; parallelize dbt with --threads and run jobs concurrently; cache dependencies; use a small auto-suspending CI warehouse. As teams grow, standardize the CI template so all repos inherit it, and scale deploy via shared git-sync/bucket that many DAGs use.

followUpQuestions: How would you store and refresh the production manifest.json so Slim CI is always accurate?
How do you give CI warehouse access with least privilege and drop per-PR schemas afterward?
How would you validate DAG structure beyond the import test (schedule, retries, cycles, task ids)?
When would you choose image-baked DAG deploys over git-sync or bucket sync?
How do you promote a risky structural dbt change (rename/type change) safely from staging to production?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: CI/CD for data pipelines lints and tests changed dbt models cheaply via Slim CI (state:modified+ with deferral to a production manifest) in an isolated schema, parses every Airflow DAG to catch broken ones before deploy, and promotes validated code across dev/stage/prod targets via git-sync, bucket sync, or dbt Cloud jobs.
keyConcepts: Slim CI: build only 'state:modified+' with '--defer --state' against a fresh production manifest.json, in an isolated CI schema.
DAG import test: build a DagBag over all DAGs and assert no import_errors so no unparseable DAG reaches the scheduler.
dbt build in CI: runs models + tests in DAG order for fail-fast, correct results on the changed subgraph.
Deploy mechanisms: dbt via dbt Cloud/git-sync/containerized runs; DAGs via git-sync sidecar, GCS/S3 sync, or image baking.
Environment promotion: per-environment targets/profiles (dev/ci/stage/prod) isolate data so CI never touches production.

commands: dbt deps   # fetch dbt packages before build/test
sqlfluff lint models/ --dialect snowflake   # lint SQL style
dbt compile --target ci   # validate refs/Jinja with no warehouse cost
dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci   # Slim CI
dbt test --select state:modified+ --state ./prod-artifacts   # run tests on changed models only
ruff check dags/   # lint Airflow DAG Python
python -c "from airflow.models import DagBag; assert not DagBag('dags/', include_examples=False).import_errors"   # DAG import test
airflow dags list   # confirm DAGs are discoverable
aws s3 sync dags/ s3://airflow-dags/prod/ --delete   # deploy DAGs to bucket (MWAA)
gsutil rsync -r dags/ gs://composer-bucket/dags/   # deploy DAGs to bucket (Composer)
interviewPoints: Slim CI builds only changed models + descendants by diffing against a production manifest, cutting CI cost/time.
The DAG import test reproduces what the scheduler does at parse time and prevents broken DAGs from jamming scheduling.
'dbt build' runs models and tests in DAG order, so CI fails fast on the changed subgraph.
Deploy dbt (dbt Cloud/git-sync/container) differs from deploy DAGs (git-sync/bucket/image bake).
Per-environment targets/profiles isolate data so CI runs in a dedicated schema and never touches production.
quickNotes: Refresh and durably store manifest.json on every prod run or Slim CI breaks.
Always pass --defer with --state so unchanged upstream refs resolve to prod, not rebuild.
Pin dbt/adapter/Airflow/provider versions in CI to exactly match the deployed environment.
Use a least-privilege CI warehouse role and a per-PR CI schema you drop afterward.
Keep DAG top-level code light so both CI parse and scheduler parse stay fast.

keyTakeaways: CI/CD for data pipelines applies lint -> test -> deploy to dbt and Airflow, but the verification is data-specific: build and test changed models in an isolated schema, and parse every DAG before it reaches the scheduler.

Slim CI ('dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state' against a production manifest.json) is the key cost/speed lever - it builds only the changed subgraph instead of the whole project, keeping CI cheap and fast as models grow.
An Airflow DAG import test (assert no DagBag import_errors) is the single most valuable CI gate, because one unparseable DAG can degrade scheduling for unrelated pipelines in production.

Deploying dbt (dbt Cloud jobs, git-sync, or containerized dbt against a prod target) is a different problem from deploying DAGs (git-sync sidecar, GCS/S3 bucket sync, or image baking), and each has its own update-speed vs immutability trade-off.

Promote pipeline code across environments with per-environment targets/profiles so CI runs in a dedicated isolated schema and never touches production, and handle structural model changes as deliberate, staged migrations.
